data.title: Are target date funds aggressive enough to give Americans retirement savings that last their lifetimes?
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

The popular default investments may need to be more aggressive in order to fund decades of retirement

The average U.S. life expectancy is 79 as of 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Will your retirement funds last long enough?

As Americans live longer, are their investments keeping up with their lifespans?

There are currently a total of $10.1 trillion in assets in 401(k) plans, and 71% of plan participants are invested in target-date funds, according to 2026 data from the Investment Company Institute. Target-date funds are investments linked to a specific year, and they adjust from riskier to more conservative as an investor gets older. One key assumption for target-date funds is that an investor's time horizon ends around age 60, at which point the portfolio shifts to a safer mix of stocks and bonds to preserve assets for retirement. However, that happens even as investors may still have decades left to live.

"Traditionally, at age 60, target-date funds go mainly into bonds. I disagree with that strategy," said Robert Pozen, a senior lecturer at Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Sloan School of Management. "People who are 60 can live to 85. People are highly likely to want to bequeath their portfolio to children - and those heirs might have 30 to 40 years until retirement."

The standard practice in target-date funds is damaging to long-term investors who don't need to live off their principal immediately, Pozen said.

How a retirement plan is invested can be just as important as how much a person saves for the future. Investments could drastically change the ultimate amount a person has to spend over the rest of their lifetime, especially as Americans are living longer and spending two or even three or more decades in retirement. The average life expectancy is 79 as of 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That's up from 20 years ago, when it was 77.8.

There's a better solution for Americans with $1 million or more in investable assets, and for households with more than $100,000 in investable assets whose noninvestment income covers their cost of living, Pozen said. These households also must have an investment horizon of 10 years or more and not need to live off their investment income. Pozen estimated that there are 6 million to 7 million American households in this group.

Those with $100,000 in a 90/10 stocks-to-bonds portfolio who reinvested all of their dividends and income would end a 30-year investment window with $1.57 million, compared with $868,000 for those with a traditional 60/40 portfolio, Pozen said.

Target-date funds are "treating everyone in the same age cohort the same, and they're not the same. They assume everyone has the same situation, and that's not true," he said.

A good default option

While target-date funds may have some flaws, other financial advisers said they are a good default option for people who may want simple, easy-to-understand investment choices.

"As a nation we're sorely uneducated when it comes to financial literacy," said Daniel Milan, managing partner at Cornerstone Financial Services. "Target-date funds are better than nothing, but nothing beats customization to your own situation."

Not everyone is well-versed in investing for retirement, and that lack of knowledge deters some people from saving for the future at all. Target-date funds have been touted as an option that simplifies the process, especially when the alternative, like choosing specific assets and what percentage of a portfolio that should be invested in them, feels daunting. These funds were also more likely to raise investors' exposure to equities compared with money-market funds, which could result in higher balances over the long term, according to TIAA Institute.

Rules of thumb

One rule of thumb in investing is that the older one gets, the more conservative the investment portfolio should be in order to prevent stock-market volatility from wrecking retirement plans. Target-date funds are based on this rule, although some advisers say near-retirees should not rely on them.

"Target-date funds can get way too conservative way too early," said Aaron Ulrich, owner of Integra Financial Planning. "For long-term time horizons, you need to be more aggressive."

Part of the problem with curtailing risk in a retirement plan is that Americans are living longer, and their portfolios need to last their entire life. "Longevity risk is real. We don't know the exact day we'll leave this earth, so longevity risk becomes a significant factor in planning," Milan said. "Equities should be a more significant factor as people are living longer."

Other financial advisers cautioned that everyone's financial situations and retirement plans are different, so general rules of thumb don't always apply.

Pozen's suggested 90/10 portfolio is just another guideline, Milan noted. "I'm not a huge fan of rules of thumb in the first place," he said. "A 60/40 rule can be a square peg in a round hole. A 90/10 rule is just creating a new rule of thumb."

James Ciamacco, senior financial adviser with Wescott Financial Advisory Group, echoed that. "It's very, very subjective. One million dollars may be enough for some people and may not be enough for other people in retirement. Defaulting for a 90/10 risk level may work for some people and not for others," he said.

"Target funds shift as you age and derisk pretty significantly as you age. That may make sense for some people," he added. "The biggest purpose of target-date funds is to give you a diversified global portfolio. You're getting a lot of exposure to different asset classes. Individuals are getting varied exposure and don't have to think about it."

Still, these funds may work better as a starting point until retirement investors are ready to customize their plans to meet their financial needs and goals.

"There's never a magic answer," Ulrich said.

-Jessica Hall

data.title: If I buy a house for $1 million in cash at 70, will I run out of money by 90?
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

Buying a house late in life means you might not reach the break-even point that would make it better financially than renting.

There's a lot to consider before you buy your retirement dream house.

Got a question about retirement? Fill out our new questionnaire or write to me directly at beth.pinsker@marketwatch.com (please put "Fix My Portfolio" in the subject line).

Dear Fix My Portfolio,

Can I afford to pay cash for a home in San Diego at 70 years old? I'm on my own, and I have approximately $770,000 in an IRA and $1 million in a brokerage. Can I spend that $1 million and still be secure until 90? Otherwise, my only income is Social Security, which I took at my full retirement age of 66 and 4 months. By the way, I pay a professional adviser a percentage each year to manage my funds.

Tired of Renting

Dear Tired,

I understand why you would want a second opinion on this question beyond your professional adviser working for a percentage. Their fee would be based on your investible assets, so if you take all of that $1 million and plunk it down on a house, their fee goes way down.

If you're using a fiduciary adviser like a certified financial planner or registered investment adviser, that shouldn't matter; they should still give you financial advice that is in your best interest. But they're human too, so at the very least it could be an awkward conversation. It might be worth it, though, because your adviser will have more information about you than you were able to provide on our handy MarketWatch Retirement Questionnaire. As with any questions for Fix My Portfolio, I can only provide general educational direction, and not specific advice for your financial situation.

But I can point out that you're not really "spending" your whole liquid savings on a house. The money doesn't go away (besides what you pay in closing costs and local taxes). Instead, you'd be making an investment, which is the same category as the stocks and bonds you might hold now. The differences are that your home values may not be predictable - and could be harder to access in an emergency. You may also face unexpected costs for maintenance and repairs.

Whether it's a good idea for you hinges on a couple of factors you'll want to consider. The first is if you're on your own and 70 now, what's your plan for aging in place in the new home? Does it have stairs? Is it in a community built for seniors?

Your long-term plan matters a lot here because the average break-even for buying a home versus renting is six years from now, according to Zillow. But with San Diego's high home values, specifically, it's 23 years. If you're only going to stay in this home until, say, 80 and then have to move to an assisted-living or nursing home, you would likely be better off renting. And if that is the trajectory you're likely to face, then you might be better off buying into a housing situation now that can adapt with your needs, like a continuing care retirement community (CCRC). With those, you'd put down cash for a buy-in and then likely pay a monthly maintenance fee like you would with a condo. You can find these communities at all sorts of price points, with the average around $400,000 and monthly fees around $3,000 to $4,000.

The long-term plan

If that's not your bag, then you could consider using some of your taxable brokerage savings to buy a long-term-care insurance policy of some sort. You indicated in your questionnaire that this wasn't on your radar right now, but if you want to "be secure until 90," as you said, then that is one way to help. You could purchase a hybrid life insurance and long-term-care policy for around $100,000 to $200,000, leaving you the funds to cover at-home care if you needed it down the road. If you don't end up needing the care (and the hope is to never get sick), then your heirs would receive a death benefit after you die.

That brings up the biggest issue to consider when buying a new house at 70 with the bulk of your savings. What is your legacy plan? In California, most estate attorneys say it's prudent to put the house in a trust, because probate in the state is a long and expensive process. The small-estate expectation for real estate is $750,000, and your $1 million property would definitely fall outside of that, not even accounting for price appreciation.

Then there's the matter of whether you want to leave any assets behind to anyone or if you would rather spend down as much as you need to by 90 or beyond. If you use your $770,000 IRA for spending, on top of Social Security, you could design a withdrawal strategy that suits your needs. Starting at 4% would give you about $30,000 this year, or $2,500 a month. You could spend about double that and run it down to zero by 90. You'll probably end up somewhere in between. But it all depends on how long you live: It could be 90, or it could be 105. And, surely, it could be tomorrow.

Most retirees fear running out of money, which is why they tend to be conservative investors and spenders, and why they build in so many contingency plans. You're not exactly going all-in with your house plan, because you have your IRA and Social Security, but you wouldn't want to set your plan for 90 and then get close and realize you're still going strong with less than you'd like to fall back on.

If you ever ran into emergencies, you could pull out equity from the house, do a reverse mortgage or sell the property and downsize - because, again, your house would be an investment that still holds value once you spend the money to buy it.

Will living in a paid-off house and keeping your spending-that is, the utility bills and taxes, groceries and dining out, healthcare, home maintenance and transportation, to name a few common routine expenses-within the parameters of Social Security plus your IRA withdrawals work for you? Or do you need more backup, like insurance or being part of a community living situation? Your feeling of security with this plan is about your own psychology, and you know that best.

You can also join the Retirement conversation in our Facebook community: Retire Better with MarketWatch.

-Beth Pinsker

data.description:
RESECURITY Joins Association of Old Crows (AOC) to Advance Electromagnetic Warfare (EW) and Spectrum Operations

RESECURITY (USA) is proud to announce our new Partner Membership with the Association of Old Crows (AOC), the premier global organization dedicated to advancing electromagnetic warfare (EW) and spectrum operations.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260808543023/en/

RESECURITY Joins Association of Old Crows (AOC) To Advance Electromagnetic Warfare (EW) and Spectrum Operations

The Association of Old Crows (AOC) is an international professional organization that began in 1964 as a forum for the exchange of technical and operational information. With over 14,000 members internationally, the AOC is dedicated to advancing the art and science of Electronic Warfare (EW), Electromagnetic Spectrum Management Operations (EMSO), Cyber Electromagnetic Activities (CEMA), Information Operations (IO), and related disciplines. The organization is headquartered in Alexandria, Virginia.

By joining this esteemed community of defense professionals, RESECURITY aims to contribute its cutting-edge technology, threat intelligence expertise, and innovation-driven approach to addressing the evolving challenges in the global electromagnetic spectrum domain and disrupting adversaries' operations.

“At RESECURITY, we are committed to delivering innovative solutions that enhance national defense capabilities. Joining AOC as a Partner Member is a natural extension of that mission,” said Shawn Loveland, CEO of RESECURITY. “We look forward to collaborating with fellow members across the Defense Industrial Base (DIB) to support the evolving needs of the EMSO community and to drive innovation to protect the U.S. and our allies.”

AOC President Anthony “Tony” Lisuzzo welcomed the announcement, stating: “We’re excited to have RESECURITY join AOC’s growing Partner Member program. Their expertise and leadership in the industry strengthen our collective ability to anticipate and respond to challenges in the electromagnetic spectrum.”

In modern military and technological strategy, cyber acts as the logic and data layer that controls, exploits, and defends the physical signals traveling through the electromagnetic spectrum (EMS). While the spectrum provides the wireless medium for communication and radar, cyber capabilities and solutions developed by RESECURITY target the software, processors, and networks riding on those waves from offensive and defensive perspectives.

This collaboration aims to shape the future of defense operations for a safer and more resilient world by expanding information sharing, enhancing threat intelligence capabilities, and fostering closer collaboration among public and private organizations responsible for national security initiatives and spectrum dominance in today’s increasingly contested electromagnetic environment.

About AOC

The Association of Old Crows (AOC) is a professional non-profit association that educates, connects, and advocates on behalf of its members and stakeholders across the global electromagnetic warfare (EW) and spectrum operations community. www.crows.org

About RESECURITY

Resecurity® is a cybersecurity company that delivers a unified endpoint protection, fraud prevention, risk management and cyber-threat intelligence platform. Known for providing best-of-breed, data-driven intelligence solutions, Resecurity’s services and platforms focus on early-warning identification of data breaches and comprehensive protection against cybersecurity risks. Founded in 2016, it has been globally recognized as one of the world’s most innovative cybersecurity companies with the mission of enabling organizations to combat cyber threats regardless of their sophistication. Most recently, by Inc. Magazine, Resecurity was named one of the Top 10 fastest-growing private cybersecurity companies in Los Angeles, California. Resecurity is a member of InfraGard National Members Alliance (INMA), AFCEA, NDIA, SIA, FS-ISAC and several American Chambers of Commerce worldwide. To learn more, visit https://resecurity.com.

data.title: Here's when Elon Musk's Starlink internet is worth the steep monthly price - and $350 startup cost
data.description:
By Genna Contino

Starlink versus fiber, cable and 5G: The smart spender's guide to 2026 internet options

Starlink is growing its subscriber base, but experts say the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk's SpaceX remains a niche option. Here's when it could make sense.

Starlink is evolving. The satellite internet provider owned and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPCX) has transitioned from an experimental service with bulky dishes to a more mainstream brand that now offers smaller hardware that's easier to install in homes.

The internet business, which now powers in-flight wifi on major airlines, was deemed the "crown jewel" of SpaceX's empire, as the company's first earnings report on Tuesday showed that Starlink's subscriber base has doubled year over year.

But broadband experts say Starlink remains a niche service for digital nomads and people living in rural areas without access to conventional internet providers such as AT&T (T) or Verizon Fios (VZ). Starlink's residential internet can be pricey: Monthly costs start at $55 for 100 megabits per second and go as high as $130. Users also must pay for the hardware, which costs $349 up front for a standard kit or can be rented for $10 a month.

In comparison, product-review site CNET shows plans with traditional providers like Xfinity (CMCSA) or Spectrum (CHTR) starting as low as $30 a month, depending on location, with equipment rentals typically ranging from $5 to $15 - although those costs may be included in the monthly price.

"Starlink can still be worth it, but at the end of the day customers are paying a premium for flexibility with this type of broadband, not because it is the cheapest product," said Tyler Cooper, editor in chief of BroadbandNow, an internet-provider comparison site.

The competition: 5G, cable and fiber

For people who live in an area with access to fiber, cable or 5G fixed-wireless internet, Starlink is a tough financial sell.

Fiber, a broadband connection that uses thin glass or plastic strands to transmit data, is the "gold standard" in 2026 due to its speed, consistency and price, said Joe Supan, a writer at CNET who focuses on broadband. "That's the strongest, most reliable connection you'll be able to get."

Earnings results: Charter sees further 'erosion' of its internet business, sending the stock sharply lower

Monthly service prices for fiber providers like Brightspeed and Metronet start at $30, according to CNET, but most households pay at least $50 a month. Cable internet providers such as Cox or Xfinity have cheaper plans in many regions, but upload and download speeds are not as fast as with fiber.

Starlink's most serious competitor in rural and suburban areas is 5G home internet, according to Cooper. "As a whole, 5G is usually cheaper, easier to install and 'good enough' for the average household," he said.

T-Mobile Magenta Max (TMUS) and Verizon wireless customers can get a discounted price of $25 to $35 for 5G home internet - but because it is wireless, it is generally slower and less reliable than cable or fiber options.

"The problem is that 5G availability can be inconsistent. We've found this can even be the case from one address to the next," Cooper said. "In areas where cellular coverage is weak or towers are congested, Starlink still has a major advantage, but this is a constantly evolving side of the business."

When Starlink makes sense

There are some instances where paying the Starlink premium could be worth it:

-- If you live where traditional wired internet lines do not exist.

-- If a local cable provider quotes you thousands of dollars to run a physical line to your property.

-- If you work remotely and cannot afford a minute of downtime. After Hurricane Helene destroyed fiber lines in western North Carolina in 2024, disrupting internet service, many households relied on Starlink after the Biden administration deployed systems to the area.

Read the fine print

No matter which internet service provider you choose, it's important to read between the lines of the marketing language and promotional rates.

"They'll show you one price, and some providers make it kind of confusing to tell what you're actually going to be paying a year from then," Supan said.

Analyst report: AT&T won't need to worry about SpaceX for 'years'

To avoid getting burned, experts recommend that consumers look beyond the flashy "speeds up to" headlines in advertisements and compare the full monthly cost of the service after accounting for expiring promotions, equipment rentals and hidden fees.

"Speed is important," Cooper said. "But reliability, upload performance, latency and long-term pricing usually matter more than the biggest number in the ad."

data.title: Social Security's funding crisis is the elephant in the room. But don't ignore the mouse.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

No one knows what Congress will do if Social Security's trust fund were actually to be depleted

Legislators could exempt current retirees from any cuts to benefits, decide to protect lower-income beneficiaries, raise payroll taxes, or even all of the above.

What age should you take Social Security?

One reader has a theory: "The possibility that Social Security will run low on funds by 2033 if Congress does not act to prevent it may be the 'elephant in the room,' no one is talking about the 'mouse in the room.' Delaying Social Security until 70 results in an increased monthly payment - and that comes with proportionally higher cost-of-living adjustments. If Social Security payments are reduced in 2033, I will still have more income than if I had filed early. A 22% reduction on $3,000 results in a higher payment than a 22% reduction on $2,000."

This scenario brings us back to the same familiar place: We can claim Social Security early, say at 62, and get those checks while we still can but with a 30% permanent lifetime reduction. Retirees might decide to do this because we think we will die relatively young, based on our own health issues and family history, or because we need the money, or because we believe Social Security is going to run low in 2033. Or, as this reader suggests, we can wait until we reach our full retirement of 67 - or even 70, when we would get roughly 8% more for each of those three years - when we might see the same cut in benefits, but on a larger check.

If any future benefit reduction is applied at the same rate to everybody's Social Security checks, delaying until 67 or 70 would indeed leave the reader with a larger monthly check, because they would be starting from a larger base amount, and it would also increase the survivor benefit for a spouse if they were to die. However, no one knows what Congress will do if Social Security's trust fund were actually to be depleted, as experts predict will happen in less than a decade. Legislators could exempt current retirees from any cuts to benefits, decide to protect lower-income beneficiaries, raise payroll taxes, or even all of the above.

The problem is that everyone is seeking certainty - about their own longevity, about what will happen to Social Security in 2033 and about the security of their retirement - but real certainty doesn't necessarily exist. Waiting until 70 is essentially buying into longevity insurance, similar to taking out a life-insurance policy. If we live well into our 80s or 90s, the larger monthly benefit can more than make up for the years we didn't collect. If we die younger, claiming earlier may prove to have been the better financial choice. Some people have a better idea of what awaits them, health-wise, than others.

The reader makes a good point about inflation and the benefits of waiting to claim. Delaying Social Security does more than boost our initial monthly benefit - it also results in higher inflation-adjusted annual increases. Because each cost-of-living adjustment is calculated as a percentage of our current benefit, someone who claims at 70 receives a proportionally larger COLA every year than a person who claims at 62. The percentage increase is the same for everyone, but the dollar amount is not. That could add up to tens of thousands of dollars over the decades.

No one knows what Congress will do if Social Security's trust fund were actually to be depleted.

Social Security faces two structural challenges over the next decade. The first is funding: Because the trust funds are invested almost entirely in low-yield government securities, they generate less income than they would under a higher-return strategy, putting pressure on reserves. The second is the lack of choice - workers cannot direct their contributions into the stock market, because the money is managed collectively. That's by design: If another Great Depression struck, Social Security would, ideally, still be there.

Two trust funds do the work of supporting retirees and those who are unable to work anymore. The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund pays monthly retirement benefits to eligible retired workers and their families. Eligibility is tied to a worker's earnings history and requires sufficient work credits - typically 40, or roughly 10 years of employment. Public confidence in the system matters, because it rests on the government's ability to hold and manage payroll taxes and meet its obligations as promised.

The Social Security Disability Insurance program, meanwhile, provides cash benefits to disabled workers and their eligible dependents. To qualify for SSDI, we must have sufficient work history and a severe, long-term disability. Both OASI and SSDI are funded primarily through payroll taxes collected under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act and the Self-Employment Contributions Act, which together support benefits for retirees, disabled workers and survivors.

The SSDI Trust Fund is currently projected to remain solvent through the end of the trustees' 75-year forecast window (roughly through 2099, which seems like forever away). But after someone receiving disability benefits reaches full retirement age, their benefits are paid out of the OASI fund - and OASI is projected to be unable to pay full benefits starting in 2033. That means disability beneficiaries could feel the effects of OASI's shortfall, too, although anything could still happen.

We are all gambling on the future. We just don't use the same chips.

data.title: My ex-husband's sister died - so why is Fidelity asking me for her death certificate?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'Part of me jokes that paying for a death certificate would be like buying a lottery ticket'

"The whole thing just seems so unusual." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I recently received a letter from Fidelity asking if I had any information about someone they believed might be related to me. Apparently, she had an account with them. I wonder if this means I'm a beneficiary of her estate.

The person in question was my former sister-in-law. She passed away about five years ago. I was married to her brother, but we've been divorced for more than 15 years. She was never married and had no children. She has several living siblings who share her last name.

The letter was addressed to me using my maiden name and sent to my current address. I find that particularly strange. I changed back to my maiden name when I divorced her brother, and I've moved since then, so I thought that was significant.

The situation is a little awkward, because my divorce was anything but pleasant.

I confirmed that she was deceased and explained that I was only her former sister-in-law. They asked me to send them a copy of her death certificate. However, Fidelity also told me they couldn't provide any information or even tell me whether I was listed as a beneficiary.

The situation is a little awkward, because my divorce was anything but pleasant. My ex and I had no children together, and after the divorce we had absolutely no contact. In fact, I didn't even know my sister-in-law had passed away.

I've been thinking about this for weeks. I can obtain a copy of her death certificate for $15 to satisfy Fidelity's request. Part of me jokes that paying for a death certificate would be like buying a lottery ticket - you never know, maybe I'd "win."

The whole thing just seems so unusual. I'm hoping you might have some insight into why Fidelity would contact a former in-law after all these years, especially when the person who died has living siblings, and when I haven't been part of the family for well over a decade.

Former Sister-in-Law

Related: 'I don't have money to pay for a death certificate': My sister refuses to probate my father's estate. What can I do?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

"It seems clear that you didn't have a close relationship with this woman."

Dear Former,

You are, I'm sorry to say, making caviar out of scrambled eggs.

Given your distant relationship with your former sister-in-law and the fact that your divorce was a difficult one, it seems unlikely that you were named as a beneficiary on her Fidelity account. It's more probable that the financial-services company is looking for confirmation that she has died so they can begin administering her account and, if appropriate, distributing any assets to the rightful beneficiaries or heirs. By some twist of fate in their search, they found you.

Leaving aside the tastelessness of comparing her death certificate to a lottery ticket, I doubt very much that it has any real-world parallels. From what you've written, it doesn't sound as though you had a particularly close relationship with her. If you had, you might be more willing to help Fidelity without wondering whether spending a modest $15 would only be worth it if you got something in return.

You're also indulging in way too much intrigue. More than likely, Fidelity hired a firm to locate potential heirs or people connected to your former sister-in-law's account or simply to verify her death before proceeding with the account. These kinds of investigators often use public records, databases, address histories and people-finder services. They just got lucky - or not - and found someone who can potentially help them.

The lottery-ticket analogy suggests that you're letting your imagination run away with you - big time. You appeared in those records because you were once related to this person through marriage. While it's possible that you were named as a beneficiary, nothing you say supports the conclusion that you were named as a beneficiary. You mention having had no contact with the family for over 15 years and not even being aware that she had died.

Don't miss: 'Don't get suckered like I did': I paid $185 to the wrong passport website. Can I get my money back?

Possible scam

Companies have a fiduciary duty to protect their clients' accounts and privacy, and those obligations don't disappear upon a client's death. Fidelity won't disclose account details until they have verified identities and determined who is entitled to those details. Fidelity may not yet have located closer relatives like parents or siblings, and you may simply have been the first verifiable lead. They are hoping you will at least point them in the right direction.

And now a warning: This could also be an elaborate scam - a scammer pretending to be from Fidelity. You are a better mark given that you are excited at the idea of getting a windfall and are already thinking about how you are going to spend the money. Scam artists do use public obituaries, public records and stolen personal data to identify recently deceased individuals and their surviving relatives, or even former relatives like you.

They then pose as reputable financial institutions, lawyers, bankers or estate officials, claiming that a wealthy person with your surname has died and imply that they may have left you a substantial inheritance. The goal is either to convince you to pay bogus administrative fees, estate taxes or other costs before the inheritance can be released, or to steal your personal information by requesting your Social Security number, date of birth or banking information.

What next? Assuming it's not a scam, providing a death certificate would help Fidelity move forward with administering the account. If you don't want to spend the $15, or the time, doing that, pass the request along to one of her siblings, or call a number on the Fidelity website and pass on their contact details. That way, the people most closely connected to her can provide the necessary information and wrap up the remainder of her estate.

The real "win" here is being given the opportunity to do the right thing.

data.title: My adult kids are big earners. Should I do a Roth conversion now so they aren't taxed as much on their inheritance?
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

Inherited IRAs can create a tax liability for heirs, but this should not be your first concern

It can be hard to decide which way to go on a Roth conversion in retirement.

Got a question about retirement? Fill out our new questionnaire or write to me directly at beth.pinsker@marketwatch.com (please put "Fix My Portfolio" in the subject line).

Dear Fix My Portfolio,

Our two children and their spouses are big earners, and I'm thinking about what we might leave behind to them. I'm 70 and have started Social Security already, and my spouse is 66 and is waiting until 70 to claim. I have a handle on Medicare surcharges and the $6,000 senior additional deduction rules. We keep our income under the New Jersey limit for tax-sheltered income, which results in no state tax for us. Whatever is left is in tax-sheltered accounts that would go to the kids and be highly taxed as opposed to our tax rate. An inherited IRA complicates the Roth solution during this period between retirement and required minimum distributions. I want to know that I have not missed something tax-wise.

Thinking Ahead

Dear Thinking Ahead,

You are definitely on the ball. You are thinking through all the conditions you should to figure out if and when you should do a Roth conversion. Perhaps what you are missing is patience.

I understand the urge to do something. You indicated in your answers to our new MarketWatch Retirement Questionnaire that you're managing your money on your own and are keeping track of most of your accounts either on your workplace retirement plan's web interface or on your own spreadsheet. This is a high level of engagement that should serve you well. You're also seeking out answers and trying to think ahead. All of this is exactly what it takes to successfully execute your retirement plan.

When retirees arrive at this place where they have everything mapped out and now it's time to just work the plan, they can get stymied. You think you're supposed to be doing something, but it's possible that what you should be doing is just proceeding onward as planned.

The worry you have about your tax rates versus the tax rates of your heirs is legitimate, but it doesn't necessarily need to be acted on right now. You and your spouse are still young. You should be considering your tax rate now versus your future tax rate, before you think about your future tax rate versus your children's. The former has one known factor - your current tax rate - while the latter has two unknowns.

In these years before you start taking required minimum distributions, which will be at age 73 for you and 75 for your spouse, Roth conversions could well make sense for you. It's possible - even likely - that your coming RMDs would push you into a higher tax bracket, and this kind of move would give you more options for tax diversification.

Say, for example, that you are in the 12% or 22% bracket now, with earnings below $211,400. That would keep you below the married threshold for the Medicare surcharges known as IRMAA. But once you start taking RMDs, even just a little extra income could push you beyond the $218,000 IRMAA cliff where the extra monthly charges start. Plus you'll pay income tax on your pretax distributions.

This is why financial advisers use the window between retirement and the start of RMDs to do multiyear Roth conversions. You can do this on your own with your spreadsheets or use do-it-yourself planning software. The key is to map out where you are in your current tax bracket and where RMDs will push you in the future. Then look at your available cash on hand to pay the extra tax due. If you can make use of the $6,000 extra senior deduction for both you and your spouse, all the better. That can offset some or all of the cost, and you can dig less deeply into your cash reserves to fund the conversion.

Thinking about your children

Once you settle all that, then you can think about your adult children. It might be a few years down the road before you act on this, however. Some retirees get to a point where their health is deteriorating or they are reaching very advanced ages and they can more clearly see what will be left after they die. At that point, you will have already secured what you need for your own living expenses and, potentially, your long-term-care needs, because you'll know the cards you've been dealt.

That's when you can think about ripping off the bandage and converting funds to Roth with an eye to the tax rate of the next generation. If you're still in the 24% bracket in 10 years, but your kids are steadily in the 32% or higher brackets, then it might make sense to convert over several years. It doesn't matter what those brackets are, as long as their bracket is above your bracket.

In his book "The Inheritance Playbook," Chad Holmes gives the example of parents who are in their 80s and have $894,000 in a tax-deferred IRA. They are in the 12% bracket, and their daughter is in the 22% bracket. If that money passes to the daughter, and she moves it to a brokerage steadily over the course of 10 years, as required, it's only worth $698,000 to her. If the parents convert it over six years, however, they'd pay $65,000 in tax and the daughter would inherit $1.1 million in a Roth account. "That would be roughly $195,000 in tax savings just by implementing some advanced tax strategies," Holmes wrote.

This may yet be something you try out, but perhaps just not right now. So all you're missing tax-wise is discipline and patience. Meanwhile, continue to keep an eye on your accounts and wait for your moment to act.

You can also join the Retirement conversation in our Facebook community: Retire Better with MarketWatch.

data.title: New to The Street Expands Global Audience, Surpassing 100,000 Subscribers Across MENA and Latin America
data.description:
International audience growth adds to New to The Street's 6 million-plus subscriber ecosystem as the company targets YouTube Diamond Creator Award status by 2028

NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / August 8, 2026 / New to The Street, one of the longest-running U.S. business television brands focused on public and private companies, announced that its subscriber audience across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and Latin America has grown to more than 100,000 subscribers, following the expansion of its programming into these international markets.

The international growth adds to New to The Street's rapidly expanding 6 million-plus subscriber ecosystem across its digital media properties, further extending the reach available to public and private companies featured across its television and digital programming.

New to The Street's international expansion includes sponsored programming broadcast across Bloomberg Television in Latin America and MENA, bringing featured company stories and executive interviews to audiences beyond the U.S. market.

Momentum is also accelerating across the company's broader social media footprint. New to The Street's Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn channels are already up more than 11% in Q3, adding to the continued expansion of its global digital audience.

The company is now targeting its next major digital milestone: reaching 10 million subscribers and YouTube Diamond Creator Award status by 2028.

"Our growth in MENA and Latin America demonstrates that the appetite for discovering companies and hearing directly from their leadership is global," said Vince Caruso, Co-Founder and CEO of New to The Street. "Surpassing 100,000 subscribers in these international markets adds another important layer to our 6 million-plus subscriber ecosystem. With our social channels already growing more than 11% in Q3, we believe the momentum is accelerating. Our goal is to reach the 10 million-subscriber Diamond milestone by 2028 as we continue expanding New to The Street globally."
